items.indep: [figure] ∠ABC = 105° and its angle bisector ray BP.
items.note: The construction gives the internal locus, as intended; if points outside the angle are included, the external angle bisector is also a locus.

steps: Assume P is restricted to the inside of ∠ABC, as the book intends.
Draw ray BC and use a protractor at B to construct ray BA so that ∠ABC = 105°.
With B as centre and compass radius 3 cm, draw an arc cutting BA at D and BC at E.
With D and E as centres and the same compass radius 3 cm, draw arcs intersecting at P inside the angle.
Draw ray BP. It bisects the 105° angle, so each half is 52.5°.
replace.answer: The required locus inside ∠ABC is the angle-bisector ray BP, with ∠ABP = ∠PBC = 52.5°.
replace.figure: ∠ABC = 105° with internal angle-bisector ray BP; P lies on the locus equidistant from arms BA and BC.

items.examiner: Points on the angle bisector are equidistant from the two arms of the angle. The required locus inside the angle is therefore its bisector ray.

items.note: Assume the required locus is the internal angle bisector within the triangle, as the book intends.

steps: At D, construct a perpendicular ray to DC on the chosen side using compass arcs; bisect the 90° angle between DC and this perpendicular ray to obtain a 45° ray DE.
On ray DE, mark E so that DE=5.9 cm, then join C to E.
At C, draw an arc of any convenient radius cutting CD and CE at X and Y.
With the same radius, draw arcs centered at X and Y to meet at Z inside ∠DCE.
Draw ray CZ; its portion from C to side DE is the required internal angle-bisector locus.
replace.answer: The required locus inside triangle CDE is the internal angle bisector of ∠DCE.
replace.figure: Triangle CDE has CD=7.6 cm, DE=5.9 cm and ∠CDE=45°. The internal bisector of ∠DCE runs from C to side DE and shows the required locus within the triangle.

items.examiner: The points equidistant from the two arms CD and CE lie on the angle bisector of ∠DCE. In the triangle, the required locus is the internal bisector shown.
